# Three nulls, three questions

Every inferential function in levi is a permutation test. The functions
differ in the object that is permuted, and the permuted object determines the
hypothesis that is tested. The null in use has to be identified before a
p-value is interpreted.

| What is permuted | Question answered | Functions |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Node labels**: expression values are exchanged among the nodes of a fixed network and layout | Is expression spatially organised on *this* network, relative to arrangements of the same values? | `levi(n_perm > 0)`, `leviGraphMoran()`, `leviGraphGetisOrd()`, `leviGraphSpectrum()`, `leviGraphWeightedTopology()` |
| **Sample labels**: condition labels are exchanged among biological replicates | Does the condition change expression in this region of the network, consistently across replicates? | `leviReplicateInference()`, `leviGraphClusterInference()`, `leviGraphTFCEInference()`, `leviGraphTFCEFreedmanLane()`, `leviBulkGraphInference()`, the `leviSingleCell*` family |
| **Edges**: the network is rewired with every node degree preserved | Does the clustering depend on the specific wiring, or does any network with these degrees show it? | `leviGraphRewiringInference()`, `leviGraphTFCERewiring()` |

The three nulls are not interchangeable.

* A node-label test does not involve the samples. It can return a small
  p-value for a single unreplicated sample, and it does not address
  replication.
* A sample-label test addresses replication only under the validity condition
  stated in the section *Validity condition for sample-label tests*.
* A sample-label test with three samples per group cannot reach p < 0.05.
  Only 20 label arrangements exist, the complementary arrangement ties the
  observed statistic, and the smallest attainable p-value is 2/20 = 0.100
  (section *Attainable p-values of small designs*).
* A rewiring test keeps the expression values fixed and addresses a
  topological question.

The examples use the bundled hub network (one hub, eight satellites) and
small simulated data, so that the vignette builds quickly. A larger `n_perm`
is used in applications.

```{r data}
hub_net <- system.file("extdata", "hub_network.dat", package = "levi")
genes   <- c("HUB", paste0("N", 1:8))

# Four control and four treated replicates on a log2 scale. The hub and its
# first two neighbours respond to treatment; the other nodes do not.
set.seed(2026)
expression <- matrix(rnorm(9 * 8, mean = 6, sd = 0.3), 9, 8,
                     dimnames = list(genes, paste0("s", 1:8)))
groups <- rep(c("control", "treated"), each = 4)
expression[c("HUB", "N1", "N2"), groups == "treated"] <-
    expression[c("HUB", "N1", "N2"), groups == "treated"] + 1.5
```

# Node-label null: the landscape test

`levi()` with `n_perm > 0` shuffles the measured node values, recalculates the
edge signals and rebuilds the landscape in every permutation. The layout is
not changed. With the default `inference_unit = "region"`, the
eight-connected regions beyond the neutral score are redetected in each
permutation, and every observed region is compared with the largest regional
mass observed under the null, taken over both directions. The maximum over
regions controls the search across regions without a further adjustment
[@Westfall1993; @Nichols2002].

```{r landscape, fig.height=5}
lfc <- rowMeans(expression[, groups == "treated"]) -
       rowMeans(expression[, groups == "control"])

set.seed(1)
res <- levi(
    expressionInput         = data.frame(ID = genes, logFC = lfc),
    networkCoordinatesInput = hub_net,
    fileTypeInput           = "dat",
    geneSymbolInput         = "ID",
    readExpColumn           = readExpColumn("logFC-logFC"),
    signal_mode             = "logfc",
    resolutionValueInput    = 20,
    smoothValueInput        = 30,
    n_perm                  = 199)

res$regions$summary[, c("Region", "Direction", "Cells", "Mass",
                        "PSpatial", "Significant")]
```

`PSpatial` is the proportion of node-label permutations, counting the
observed arrangement, in which the largest regional mass anywhere on the
landscape was at least as large as the mass of the region. It is conditional
on the network and on the layout: the layout is part of the test, and a
different layout of the same graph defines a different test. `PSpatial` does
not address replication, because the sample labels are not permuted.

`leviRegionGenes()` ranks the nodes that support each region. The ranking is
an aid to interpretation and not a gene-level test:

```{r region-genes}
head(leviRegionGenes(res, top_n = 3))
```

## The legacy cell mode

`inference_unit = "cell"` tests every occupied grid cell and adjusts the two
directional families jointly with `p_adjust_method` (`"BY"` by default).
Adjacent grid cells are strongly correlated, which makes this adjustment
conservative. The mode is retained because the graphical interface draws its
contours from it and for comparison with earlier versions. The regional test
is the default.

# Sample-label null: biological replication

When biological replicates exist, the sample labels can be permuted.
`leviReplicateInference()` recomputes the gene-level log fold change, rebuilds
the landscape and redetects the regions for every arrangement of the
condition labels. The regions are the same objects as in the node-label test,
and the p-value refers to the sample-label null.

```{r replicate, fig.height=5}
set.seed(1)
rep_res <- leviReplicateInference(
    expression, groups, test = "treated", control = "control",
    networkCoordinatesInput = hub_net, fileTypeInput = "dat",
    resolutionValueInput = 20, smoothValueInput = 30)

rep_res$regions$summary[, c("Region", "Direction", "Mass", "PSpatial",
                            "Significant")]
rep_res$metadata[c("permutation_exact", "possible_permutations", "p_floor")]
```

With four replicates per group there are `choose(8, 4) = 70` distinct label
arrangements, and the test enumerates all of them (`permutation_exact` is
`TRUE`). Exchanging every label negates the fold changes, and the statistic is
the maximum over both directions, so an arrangement and its complement give
the same value. The smallest attainable p-value is therefore 2/70 = 0.029
(`metadata$p_floor`).

The same null is used by the graph-native tests, which do not require a
layout. `leviGraphTFCEInference()` fits a limma moderated t statistic per
gene [@Smyth2004] and integrates it over thresholds with threshold-free
cluster enhancement [@Smith2009], with the network components as clusters:

```{r tfce}
tfce <- leviGraphTFCEInference(
    expression, groups, hub_net, test = "treated", control = "control")
tfce$statistic[order(tfce$statistic$PGlobal), ][1:4, ]
```

`PGlobal` compares the TFCE score of each gene with the maximum over all genes
and both directions in every permutation. This controls the family-wise error
rate across genes.

## Paired designs and covariates

The argument `blocks` (donor, batch, litter) restricts the permutation of
labels to within blocks, and the block enters the linear model as a fixed
effect. When the nuisance covariates are continuous or numerous,
`leviGraphTFCEFreedmanLane()` permutes the residuals of the nuisance-only
model instead of the labels [@Freedman1983; @Winkler2014]. The single-cell
functions aggregate cells into donor pseudobulks and permute donors, jointly
across cell types, so that cells are not treated as replicates [@Squair2021].

# Validity condition for sample-label tests

A sample-label test is a replication test only when the network and its gene
set are fixed independently of the labels that are permuted. When the genes
are selected on the same labels and then held fixed during the permutations,
the observed statistic has been maximised over the gene universe, whereas the
permuted statistics have not. The observed value is then compared with a null
distribution that lacks the selection step, and the test rejects under the
global null.

The simulation reported in the manuscript and in `vignette("levi_validation")`
quantifies this. The data were 2000 independent standard normal genes with no
effect. The 30 genes with the largest absolute t statistic were placed on the
30-node `medusa` network, with 200 datasets per design. The procedure that
held the selected genes fixed during the permutations rejected at
alpha = 0.05 in

* 85 to 87 % of the datasets with 4 vs 4 samples and exact enumeration
  (regional test 0.870, Wilson 95 % limits 0.816 to 0.910; graph TFCE 0.850,
  0.794 to 0.893), where the benchmark is 1/35 = 0.029, and
* 99 to 100 % of the datasets with 8 vs 8 samples and Monte Carlo sampling
  with 199 draws (regional test 0.990, 0.964 to 0.997; graph TFCE 1.000,
  0.981 to 1.000), where the benchmark is 0.05.

Re-selecting the genes inside each permutation (closed loop) gave rejection
rates of 0.015 to 0.060, and selecting the genes on separate samples (split
sample) gave 0.045 to 0.055. The Wilson 95 % limits of these rates cover the
respective benchmark (1/35 for exact tests, 0.05 for Monte Carlo), with one
exception: the split-sample TFCE row with 200 datasets (11 of 200, limits
0.031 to 0.096), for which 2000 datasets gave 0.034 (0.027 to 0.042). The
complete table is in `vignette("levi_validation")`, section *Selection before
testing*. The simulation selects values on a fixed topology. It does not model
selection of the connectivity.

Three designs satisfy the condition.

1. **A priori network.** The pathway or network and its gene set are fixed
   before the data are inspected (for example a KEGG pathway).
2. **Closed-loop selection.** The complete selection, and the construction of
   the network from it, are repeated inside every permutation, on the
   permuted labels. Selection by rank (a fixed number of genes with the
   smallest p-values or the largest absolute statistics) is required. A
   selection that includes an effect-size cut, such as an absolute fold change
   above a threshold, can return an empty network under permutation. In the
   manuscript analysis of GSE10072 with such a filter, 832 of 999 permuted
   fits left fewer than three connected genes. No exported function of levi
   re-selects genes inside the permutations; the loop is written by the
   analyst around the statistic of interest.
3. **Split-sample selection.** The genes are selected on one subset of the
   samples and the test is performed on the remaining samples. The label
   permutations are applied to the test samples only, and the floor of the
   design is that of the test samples.

Results on a network built from genes selected on the tested samples are
descriptive. This applies to the sample-label regional tests, to the graph
cluster and TFCE tests and to the rewiring tests on such a network. The
node-label test remains a valid statement about the spatial organisation of
that fixed network and layout (section *Node-label null*), and it is not
evidence of replication.

# Attainable p-values of small designs

The smallest p-value that a permutation test can report depends on the number
of distinct arrangements and on the statistic. Let n be the number of distinct
label arrangements of a two-group design. For the two-sided maximum
statistic used by the sample-label tests of levi, the attainable floor is

* 2/n, for an exactly enumerated design in which every exchangeable block is
  balanced (the complementary arrangement, with every label exchanged, gives
  the same maximum over both directions and ties the observed value),
* 1/n, for an exactly enumerated design that is not balanced within every
  block, and
* 1/(n_perm + 1), for Monte Carlo sampling of n_perm arrangements.

The floor is stored in `metadata$p_floor` of every sample-label result.
When the floor exceeds the significance level, the function issues a warning
that no result can be significant at that level. The table gives n and the
floor for common balanced designs.

| Design | Arrangements (n) | Smallest p (2/n) |
|:--|--:|--:|
| 3 vs 3, unblocked | 20 | 0.100 |
| 4 vs 4, unblocked | 70 | 0.029 |
| 4 donors, paired (within-donor swaps) | 16 | 0.125 |
| 5 donors, paired | 32 | 0.0625 |
| 6 donors, paired | 64 | 0.031 |
| 8 donors, paired | 256 | 0.0078 |

Three further properties follow from the definition.

* For the 4 vs 4 unblocked design the floor, 0.029, is below 0.05, so no
  warning is issued. The attainable p-values are 2j/70, and the only value
  that rejects at 0.05 is the floor itself.
* The per-direction columns `POver` and `PUnder` are compared with the null of
  one direction. They keep the floor 1/n and are not adjusted across the two
  directions.
* The p-values of node-label tests are not limited by the number of sample
  arrangements, because the sample labels are not permuted. Their floor is
  1/(n_perm + 1). The size of the node-label permutation space is not a
  reason to read these values as evidence of replication; the reason is that
  the sample labels are not permuted.

# Edge null: dependence on the wiring

The rewiring tests keep the gene scores fixed and generate networks with the
same degree sequence by degree-preserving edge swaps [@Maslov2002]. The null
hypothesis is that the observed clustering is explained by the degree
sequence alone.

```{r rewiring}
scores <- setNames(tfce$statistic[["T"]], tfce$statistic$Gene)
set.seed(1)
rew <- leviGraphRewiringInference(scores, hub_net, threshold = 1.5,
                                  n_perm = 199)
rew$regions$summary[, c("Region", "Direction", "Nodes", "Mass", "PSpatial")]
```

On a star network no edge swap preserves the degrees and changes the graph,
so every null draw equals the observed network and the test is uninformative
by construction. On networks in which several graphs share a degree sequence,
the test distinguishes responding genes that are hubs from responding genes
that are connected to one another. The test is conditional on the gene
scores; on a network built from genes selected on the tested samples, its
result is descriptive.

# Autocorrelation on the graph

`leviGraphMoran()` and `leviGraphGetisOrd()` are graph analogues of the
spatial statistics Moran's I [@Moran1950] and Getis-Ord G [@Getis1992]. Both
use the node-label null. The local tables carry a Benjamini-Hochberg
adjustment across nodes [@Benjamini1995], and the `Significant` flag of the
Getis-Ord table uses the two-sided adjusted p-value.

```{r moran}
set.seed(1)
moran <- leviGraphMoran(scores, hub_net, n_perm = 199)
moran$global
head(leviGraphGetisOrd(scores, hub_net, n_perm = 199, seed = 1)[,
    c("Gene", "GiStar", "PTwoSided", "PAdjusted", "Class")])
```

# Parallel execution

Every permutation function accepts `BPPARAM`. The default, `SerialParam()`,
runs the null in the calling process; `BiocParallel::MulticoreParam()` or
`SnowParam()` distribute it over workers. All random numbers are drawn before
the workers start, so the result is identical for any back-end under the same
seed.

```{r parallel, eval=FALSE}
library(BiocParallel)
tfce_par <- leviGraphTFCEInference(
    expression, groups, hub_net, test = "treated", control = "control",
    n_perm = 999, BPPARAM = MulticoreParam(4))
```

# Reporting checklist

1. State the null: node labels, sample labels or edges.
2. Report the number of permutations, whether the enumeration was exact and
   the attainable floor (`permutation_exact`, `possible_permutations`,
   `p_floor`).
3. For landscape tests, report the network source, the layout algorithm and
   seed, the resolution and the smoothing. A different layout defines a
   different test.
4. For sample-label tests, report the blocking structure and the p-value
   floor of the design.
5. State how the network and its gene set were chosen: fixed a priori,
   selected inside each permutation, selected on separate samples, or
   selected on the tested samples. In the last case, report the sample-label
   and graph results as descriptive.
6. Interpret node-label significance as a statement about spatial
   organisation, and not as evidence that an effect replicates.
7. When replicates exist, report a sample-label test next to the landscape:
   `leviReplicateInference()` for the same regions and
   `leviGraphTFCEInference()` as the layout-free test, under the validity
   condition above. On a network in which most genes respond, the
   area-weighted node-label statistic does not separate the observed
   arrangement from shuffled arrangements (p = 0.21 to 0.89 on the Kang
   networks analysed in the manuscript), and its value can fall below 0.05
   under neighbouring parameter settings.
